turns.en: A few months ago, I sat down with Jensen Huang, the co-founder and CEO of NVIDIA, one of the world's most valuable companies, and we released that conversation as an audio episode of How I Built This back in May of this year. Now, Jensen is obviously in the news, and it is a challenging time for him and for NVIDIA. And this interview doesn't deal with any of that, but what you will see, I hope, is a fuller picture of who he is. This is a conversation about his family and his upbringing, his demanding and even difficult approach to leadership, and why he says he wouldn't ever want to build NVIDIA again. So, judge for yourself. I hope you find this conversation interesting at the very least. And here it is, my conversation with Jensen Huang recorded in April of 2026.
turns.zh: 几个月前，我与 NVIDIA 联合创始人兼 CEO、全球市值最高的公司之一掌门人黄仁勋坐下来聊了聊，并将那次对话作为《我如何建立它》的音频节目于今年五月发布。如今，黄仁勋显然身处新闻焦点，对他和 NVIDIA 来说都是艰难时期。这次访谈并不涉及那些，但我希望你能从中更全面地了解他这个人。这是一场关于他的家庭与成长、他严苛甚至苛刻的领导风格，以及他为何说再也不想重建 NVIDIA 的对话。所以，你自己判断吧。我希望至少你会觉得这场对话有趣。下面就是我在 2026 年 4 月录制的与黄仁勋的对话。

turns.en: You have been on the record as basically saying if you've been asked, would you do this again? Would you do this all over again? And I'm sort of paraphrasing sort of version of no. I would do it again.
turns.zh: 你曾公开说过，如果被问到“你会再来一次吗？你会从头再做一遍吗？”我大致转述一下，你的回答是“不，我不会”。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: So, can you explain that? I mean we've sort of have the outlines of all of the troughs, and there are a lot of troughs. And I'm trying to even imagine like quarterly earning calls in 2007 when your stock price is in the toilet and you're putting all this money into CUDA and people are saying what? I'm trying to figure out how you can do that as a publicly traded company, withstand the pressure, and as you say, the embarrassment of
turns.zh: 你能解释一下吗？我的意思是，我们已经大致了解所有低谷的轮廓，而且有很多低谷。我甚至试着想象 2007 年的季度财报电话会议，当时你的股价跌入谷底，你却把大量资金投入 CUDA，人们都在说“什么？”我试图理解你作为一家上市公司如何做到这一点，承受压力，以及如你所说，那种尴尬——

turns.en: It was embarrassing, it was humiliating. You're the only face that everybody hates. Your employees are probably embarrassed for you. Your question about doing it again. Most people when I just think they're being dishonest. So let me just tell you why. When somebody asks me, would I do this again? If your question is knowing how NVIDIA turned out, knowing the contribution we've made to the world, knowing the consequence of the company today, how it impacts so many different industries, the joy that we brought to our employees, all of the benefits that we have accrued as a result of our success. Do I love those things? The answer is yes. But that wasn't the question. The question is, I mean, who doesn't? And so but the question is suppose I knew everything then that I now know how hard it is.
turns.zh: 很尴尬，很丢人。你是所有人唯一憎恨的对象。你的员工可能都为你感到难堪。你问我会不会再来一次。我觉得大多数人回答时都不诚实。所以让我告诉你为什么。当有人问我“你会再来一次吗？”如果你的问题是“知道 NVIDIA 后来变成这样，知道我们对世界做出的贡献，知道公司今天的影响力，它如何影响这么多不同的行业，我们给员工带来的快乐，我们因成功而获得的所有好处。我喜欢这些东西吗？”答案是肯定的。但这不是问题所在。问题是，谁不喜欢呢？所以问题是，假设我当时就知道现在所知道的一切，知道这有多难。

turns.en: And you didn't know what the outcome would be.
turns.zh: 而你当时并不知道结果会怎样。

turns.en: That's right. For example, I now know how hard it is to build NVIDIA. I now know how hard it is to build CUDA. I now know how hard it is to get everybody in the world to use CUDA. And I now know how long it took. And all of the pain and suffering and all the embarrassment and humiliation and all the setbacks and you compress all of that and you just told that 30-year-old kid, listen, this is going to take a lot longer than you think. Whatever however fast you thought your company was going to be successful, it's not going to be anything like that. And you're going to be the person who delivers most of the most horrific financial return news that anybody's ever explained. You'll have activists come after your company, you'll have, you know, so and so forth. You'll be going out of business, you'll have to lay people off. You have to deliver such enormously bad news. You have to do all of that. Would you start again? The answer, absolutely not. And so I think a lot of people forget that the pain and suffering necessary, the endurance necessary to do something great is because you're always looking forward and forgetting the past.
turns.zh: 没错。比如，我现在知道建立 NVIDIA 有多难。我现在知道建立 CUDA 有多难。我现在知道让全世界所有人都用上 CUDA 有多难。我现在知道这花了多长时间。所有的痛苦、折磨、尴尬、羞辱、挫折，你把所有这些压缩起来，然后告诉那个 30 岁的孩子：听着，这比你想象的要花长得多的时间。无论你以为你的公司会多快成功，都不会是那样。你将成为那个向所有人宣布最可怕的财务回报消息的人。会有激进投资者来找你公司的麻烦，会有这样那样的事。你会濒临破产，你不得不裁员。你不得不宣布如此糟糕的消息。你不得不做所有这些事。你还会重新开始吗？答案是，绝对不会。所以我认为很多人忘记了，成就伟大事业所必需的痛苦和忍耐，是因为你总是向前看，忘记过去。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: I spent all my time forgetting yesterday. In fact, right now as we're talking, it is really quite hard for me to resurface those memories and resurface those feelings. And the reason for that is I spent all of my time, all of my life trying to forget yesterday.
turns.zh: 我把所有时间都花在忘记昨天上。事实上，就在我们谈话的此刻，我很难重新浮现那些记忆和那些感受。原因是我把所有时间、我的一生都用来试图忘记昨天。

turns.en: Right. Does it trigger tension?
turns.zh: 对。这会引发紧张吗？

turns.en: Yeah, yeah, it triggers anxiety, it triggers yeah, I that's why I don't love talking about my past because I spent all my time forgetting it so that you can get back on that horse. That's in fact, what do they teach athletes? Forget the last point.
turns.zh: 是的，是的，会引发焦虑，会引发——是的，这就是为什么我不喜欢谈论我的过去，因为我把所有时间都用来忘记它，这样你才能重新上马。事实上，他们教运动员什么？忘记上一分。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: It's about forgetting. And so a lot of people don't realize that if you want to be a marathoner, if you want NVIDIA's a you know, NVIDIA high tech is a marathon sprint. And so you're full out every single day and it did take 34 years. And so and we're still at it. And so I think the challenge is how do you look forward with promise and enthusiasm and deep belief meanwhile, all the pain and suffering and the setbacks that's, you know, to somehow learn from it, codify that learning, make sure it goes into every fiber in your body, but leave it behind. Just let it go.
turns.zh: 关键在于忘记。所以很多人没有意识到，如果你想成为马拉松选手，如果你想——NVIDIA 是一家——你知道，NVIDIA 的高科技是一场马拉松冲刺。所以你每天都要全力以赴，这确实花了 34 年。而我们仍在努力。所以我认为挑战在于，如何带着希望、热情和坚定信念向前看，同时，所有的痛苦、折磨和挫折，你要以某种方式从中学习，将学习编码，确保它融入你身体的每根纤维，但把它抛在身后。就让它过去吧。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And so that's kind of
turns.zh: 所以这就是——

turns.en: I think it's a really healthy way to see the world. I think it's hard and it requires a lot of discipline. And now I'm going to ask you about the past again, right? But I mean I again, yeah, I understand. I mean the sacrifice, right? I mean you've got a family. Like you probably missed a lot of things. You probably did 12-hour days, seven days a week for years. Um and after after you sort of really began to focus on AI, it it doubled again. I mean it was a it was a and you were you'd already been here a long time. Um and so I imagine this personal sacrifice on your health probably. You probably didn't get to exercise every day or do I mean you probably didn't get to eat every day. I mean there were things you probably didn't get to see your family as much as you wanted to see. All those things.
turns.zh: 我认为这是一种非常健康的看待世界的方式。我认为这很难，需要很强的自律。现在我又要问你过去的事了，对吧？但我的意思是，我再次理解。我是说牺牲，对吧？你有家庭。你可能错过了很多事情。你可能多年每周七天每天工作 12 小时。嗯，在你真正开始专注于 AI 之后，它又翻倍了。我是说，那是一种——而且你已经在这里很久了。嗯，所以我想象这对你的健康造成了个人牺牲。你可能没能每天锻炼，或者——我是说你可能没能每天吃饭。我是说，有些事情你可能没能像你希望的那样多见到家人。所有那些事。

turns.en: All true. All true. And during the time when the kids were still young, I was finishing my masters at Stanford. And so I was busy on multiple levels and when the kids were still young I missed all their karate tournaments. I missed a lot. I missed a lot. Yeah. And we didn't have laptops at the time so you couldn't really do work at home for many years.
turns.zh: 都是真的。都是真的。在孩子们还小的时候，我正在斯坦福完成硕士学位。所以我在多个层面上都很忙，当孩子们还小的时候，我错过了他们所有的空手道比赛。我错过了很多。我错过了很多。是的。而且当时我们没有笔记本电脑，所以很多年你都无法在家工作。

turns.en: There weren't obviously any iPhones, and the internet had barely gotten off the ground yet, and Windows 95 hadn't come, so most of us didn't have PCs at home. If you wanted to do any work, you had to come to work. So that was back in the old days. I don't know that I've ever asked them what it was like on the receiving side of it. But if you were going to build a company, you need somebody strong and you need somebody amazing like my wife. She took care of everything. Lori took care of everything. Took care of me, took care of the kids, took care of everything. I don't remember her even one time, one nanosecond or even one instance—I don't think she's ever mentioned it once. That's the gift that she gave me. Both kids love NVIDIA to their core.
turns.zh: 显然那时没有 iPhone，互联网才刚刚起步，Windows 95 还没问世，所以我们大多数人家里都没有电脑。如果你想做任何工作，都得去办公室。那是旧时光了。我不知道是否问过他们接收方的感受。但如果你要创办一家公司，你需要一个坚强的人，一个像我的妻子那样了不起的人。她照顾了一切。Lori 照顾了一切。照顾我，照顾孩子，照顾一切。我不记得她有过一次、一纳秒或一个实例——我想她从未提过一次。那是她给我的礼物。两个孩子都深爱着 NVIDIA。

turns.en: And both work here.
turns.zh: 而且两人都在这里工作。

turns.en: Both work here. They both went off to their own careers for a while, and we were lucky to attract them back. Both kids have read every shareholder letter, gone to every shareholder meeting, been to every single conference that I've ever done.
turns.zh: 两人都在这里工作。他们各自发展事业了一段时间，我们很幸运能吸引他们回来。两个孩子都读过每一封股东信，参加过每一次股东大会，出席过我做的每一场会议。

turns.en: Hm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: I've missed most of theirs. They've been to all of mine. Both of them love NVIDIA since they were born. Spencer's 35, Madison's 34, and the company's 33 years old. That kind of puts it in perspective.
turns.zh: 我错过了他们的大部分活动。他们却参加了我所有的活动。他们俩从出生起就热爱 NVIDIA。Spencer 35 岁，Madison 34 岁，公司已经 33 年了。这让人有了更直观的感受。

turns.en: Hm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: They've had NVIDIA in their lives the whole time. And despite the fact that I was gone a lot, they found a way to always love the company. I'm really lucky.
turns.zh: 他们一生都有 NVIDIA 相伴。尽管我经常不在家，他们总能找到方式热爱这家公司。我真的很幸运。

turns.en: Your story to me is just a story—and even now in a different way—it's a story of pressure.
turns.zh: 你的故事对我来说就是一个故事——即使现在以不同的方式——也是一个关于压力的故事。

turns.en: Hm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Right? And now it's like you did not intend or anticipate that this is going to be the company it is. And it is where it is. And it's not just NVIDIA in Santa Clara, in Santa Clara County, in Northern California, in California. Its importance is global. And that's a lot of responsibility.
turns.zh: 对吧？现在的情况是，你并未打算或预料到它会成为这样的公司。而它确实如此。它不仅仅是圣克拉拉、圣克拉拉县、北加州、加州的 NVIDIA。它的重要性是全球性的。那是很大的责任。

turns.en: Yeah. And humility is helpful.
turns.zh: 是的。谦逊是有帮助的。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Being grounded is helpful. Yeah. Not doing this job from a yacht is helpful.
turns.zh: 脚踏实地是有帮助的。是的。不在游艇上做这份工作是有帮助的。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And the fact that the company was built stone by stone with the people that are here. And everybody else, everybody so grounded. I think it's helpful, but you also have to realize that the company also evolved over 30 years. You know it recently. But this is one of the oldest technology companies in the world.
turns.zh: 而且公司是一砖一石地与这里的人一起建立起来的。还有其他人，每个人都如此脚踏实地。我认为这很有帮助，但你也必须意识到，公司也经历了 30 年的演变。你最近才了解它。但这是世界上最古老的技术公司之一。

turns.en: I know that we have talked a lot about you and your life. But the guy who wrote a biography of you and Nvidia, Steven Witt, said you were one of the most challenging people to report on because you generally don't like to talk about yourself.
turns.zh: 我知道我们谈了很多关于你和你的生活。但为你和 Nvidia 写传记的 Steven Witt 说，你是最难报道的人之一，因为你通常不喜欢谈论自己。

turns.en: Great reservation doing so, yes.
turns.zh: 非常保留，是的。

turns.en: And I wonder is that because you just find it to be self-aggrandizing or I don't know just you find it to be you know being self-reflective. I mean going back to what you said about forgetting everything that happened and just moving forward. Is that part of it? Is it part—I notice that when you talk about your kids or even your parents and the struggles and sacrifice they make, you do get a little bit emotional and I wonder whether part of not liking to talk about yourself is maybe some of that.
turns.zh: 我想知道，是因为你觉得这自我夸大，还是我不知道，只是你觉得自我反思。我的意思是回到你说的忘记发生的一切，只是向前看。这是部分原因吗？是不是部分——我注意到当你谈到你的孩子，甚至你的父母和他们的奋斗与牺牲时，你确实有点情绪化，我想知道不喜欢谈论自己是否部分源于此。

turns.en: Yeah, even that's a hard question. Why don't I like talking about myself? I didn't do anything by myself. Somebody else decided where I went to college. I was clever to maneuver myself next to the best girl in school. That was just smart calculus and smart strategy. It was maybe the smartest thing I ever did. I was fortunate to have two amazing friends, Chris and Curtis. I'm surrounded by amazing computer scientists here. I made a lot of good decisions. I've made a large number of lesser good decisions. I just don't find any of that to be very special or that interesting. It barely interests myself. And so I think I'm just uncomfortable talking about it, maybe. I don't know why, guy. I don't know why. Maybe I need therapy to help me figure it out.
turns.zh: 是的，即使那也是很难的问题。为什么我不喜欢谈论自己？我没有独自做成任何事。别人决定了我去哪里上大学。我很聪明地让自己靠近学校里最优秀的女孩。那只是聪明的算计和聪明的策略。那可能是我做过的最聪明的事。我很幸运有两个了不起的朋友，Chris 和 Curtis。我周围都是了不起的计算机科学家。我做了很多好的决定。我也做了大量不那么好的决定。我只是不觉得那些有什么特别或有趣。它几乎不引起我自己的兴趣。所以我想我只是谈论它时不自在，也许。我不知道为什么，伙计。我不知道为什么。也许我需要心理治疗来帮我弄清楚。

turns.en: I want to ask you about your childhood because I know that you were born in Taiwan, but you spent some of it in Thailand.
turns.zh: 我想问问你的童年，因为我知道你出生在台湾，但有一部分时间在泰国度过。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And there was the story is that there was like there's political unrest in Thailand at the time. This is in the early '70s and your parents sent you and your brother to Kentucky to go to school there. What do you know about—you were only 10—what do you know about why Kentucky? How did that happen?
turns.zh: 有故事说当时泰国有政治动荡。那是 70 年代初，你的父母把你和你的兄弟送到肯塔基州去上学。你知道什么——你当时只有 10 岁——你知道为什么是肯塔基吗？那是怎么发生的？

turns.en: So it was 1973 and periodically Thailand would have a coup. And this just happened to be one of them. They had to send us away. And there weren't that many boarding schools in America that would take international students, but somehow Oneida Baptist Institute in Kentucky, Clay County, Kentucky. Population I think was 600 at the time. Today their population 600. Incredible town, little tiny town, no stop light. And there was a school on this mound on this small mound, kind of a small hill. But probably the most important feature was that it was a boarding school and it was incredibly affordable.
turns.zh: 那是 1973 年，泰国时不时会发生政变。这恰好是其中一次。他们不得不把我们送走。美国没有那么多寄宿学校接收国际学生，但不知怎么的，肯塔基州克莱县的 Oneida Baptist Institute。我记得当时人口是 600。今天人口还是 600。不可思议的小镇，非常小的镇，没有红绿灯。学校在一个小土丘上，像个小山丘。但最重要的特点可能是它是一所寄宿学校，而且非常负担得起。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Because my parents didn't have much money and here we are. They were in Southeast Asia trying to put kids in school in America. So you could just imagine it was beyond their reach. And so they found the most affordable boarding school in America for us. And so we went there and every kid that lived there had to work. And so they had no custodians. And so we had to take care of ourselves and my job was to clean the bathrooms. And apparently I was the youngest kid that ever went there. I still am, I think.
turns.zh: 因为我父母没有多少钱，而我们就在这里。他们在东南亚，试图把孩子送到美国上学。你可以想象那超出了他们的能力。所以他们为我们找到了美国最负担得起的寄宿学校。我们去了那里，每个住在那里的孩子都必须工作。他们没有管理员。所以我们必须照顾自己，我的工作是打扫厕所。显然我是去过那里最年轻的孩子。我想我现在仍然是。

turns.en: Did you—were you 10?
turns.zh: 你——你当时 10 岁吗？

turns.en: I was nine when I went there.
turns.zh: 我去那里时九岁。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: I've got great memories of it. I loved the place. It was a tough school because they invited kids from all walks of life. And so my roommate was—I was nine and my roommate was 16. And it was a tough school because none of the closets had doors and none of the drawers, because everything had to be out in the open. You just don't know what the kids are going to have.
turns.zh: 我有很多美好的回忆。我喜欢那个地方。那是一所严格的学校，因为他们邀请来自各行各业的孩子。我的室友——我九岁，我的室友 16 岁。那是一所严格的学校，因为没有一个衣柜有门，没有一个抽屉有门，因为一切都必须公开。你根本不知道孩子们会有什么。

turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.en: Yeah, it was incredible.
turns.zh: 是的，太不可思议了。

turns.en: Um.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: That was yeah. Welcome to America.
turns.zh: 那就是，是的。欢迎来到美国。

turns.en: Yeah, right.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。

turns.en: But I loved it. It was incredible. I was on the swim team and the soccer team.
turns.zh: 但我喜欢它。太不可思议了。我参加了游泳队和足球队。

turns.en: And then afterwards the coach would take you out to give you a treat. And I remember recording—we used to record a tape and send it back to our parents. But long distance phone calls cost too much money. So we never spoke to them live until they came to the United States almost two years later. We would record what happened this last month, send it to them by mail. They'd record it, send it back to us. And we were ping-ponging like that for a couple of years. And I remember telling them that after the swim meet, the coach took us to this incredible restaurant with lights everywhere like from outer space and all the food was in boxes—and it was McDonald's.
turns.zh: 然后之后教练会带我们出去，给我们一点奖励。我记得我们录音——我们过去会录一盘磁带寄给父母。但长途电话太贵了。所以直到他们将近两年后来到美国，我们才第一次和他们实时通话。我们会录下这个月发生的事情，邮寄给他们。他们录好再寄回来给我们。就这样来回寄了几年。我记得我告诉他们，游泳比赛之后，教练带我们去了一个不可思议的餐厅，到处都是灯，像来自外太空，所有食物都装在盒子里——那是麦当劳。

turns.en: It's McDonald's, yeah.
turns.zh: 是麦当劳，没错。

turns.en: Which was magical.
turns.zh: 那真是太神奇了。

turns.en: Yeah, incredible. You eventually reunite with your family in Portland, which is where your dad settles and you grew up there and you went on to—this is the early late '70s Oregon State. And this is like the beginning of what would become the computer revolution. You are studying electrical engineering cuz I don't think they had a computer science program
turns.zh: 是的，不可思议。你最终在波特兰与家人团聚，你父亲在那里定居，你在那里长大，然后你去了——这是70年代末的俄勒冈州立大学。这就像是后来计算机革命的起点。你学的是电气工程，因为我觉得当时他们还没有计算机科学专业

turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 没有。

turns.en: there at the time. And that's also where you would meet the person who would become your wife.
turns.zh: 当时那里没有。那也是你遇到后来成为你妻子的人的地方。

turns.en: Yeah, so when I was in high school, I wasn't very outgoing and so I didn't have that many friends. All my best friends were in a club together. We were in two clubs. One club was the math club and then the other club was the computer club.
turns.zh: 是的，所以当我上高中时，我不是很外向，所以没有很多朋友。我所有的好朋友都在一个俱乐部里。我们参加了两个俱乐部。一个是数学俱乐部，另一个是计算机俱乐部。

turns.en: Nice.
turns.zh: 不错。

turns.en: Cuz the same four kids.
turns.zh: 因为同样的四个孩子。

turns.en: Guys, yeah.
turns.zh: 伙计们，是的。

turns.en: The same four kids, right. And my best friend in high school, I asked him where he was going to college and he said Oregon State. And he asked me where I was going to college and never crossed my mind to go anywhere out of town for—the idea of going to a great university never crossed my mind. So he said he was going to Oregon State. I said, yeah, that sounds great. I'll go to Oregon State. And so we were roommates and there we both enrolled in electrical engineering. And our lab—the class had 200, must have 250 kids. It was a big class. And there were three girls. And so I know the story—what, you know, is a super pretty girl and I was probably the youngest kid in class then as well. And I went to school rather early. I skipped two grades in school, so I was just a tiny kid. And we were in lab together and I found a way to arrange myself into the same lab as her, same group as her, and so we became lab partners and here we are.
turns.zh: 同样的四个孩子，没错。我高中最好的朋友，我问他要去哪所大学，他说俄勒冈州立大学。他问我要去哪所大学，我从来没想过要去外地——上名牌大学的想法从未在我脑海中闪过。所以他说要去俄勒冈州立大学。我说，好啊，听起来不错。我也去俄勒冈州立大学。于是我们成了室友，我们都报了电气工程。我们的实验室——那个班有200人，肯定有250人。是个大班。只有三个女生。所以我知道那个故事——有个超级漂亮的女孩，我当时可能是班上最小的孩子。我上学很早。我跳了两级，所以我只是个小孩子。我们一起在实验室，我想办法把自己安排到和她同一个实验室，同一个小组，于是我们成了实验室搭档，然后就有了我们。

turns.en: Yeah. Both of you after you graduated moved to California. This is like 1984 ish, I think, which is the center of the revolution, right? I mean your first job was with AMD.
turns.zh: 是的。你们俩毕业后都搬到了加州。我想这是1984年左右，那是革命的中心，对吧？我的意思是你的第一份工作是在AMD。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And I think she also had a job
turns.zh: 我想她也有工作

turns.en: Silicon Graphics.
turns.zh: 硅谷图形公司。

turns.en: Silicon Graphics, yeah. And you were—I mean you were what did it look like to design computer chips in 1984? I mean was it CAD? Was it what did that look like—what did that actually physically entail?
turns.zh: 硅谷图形公司，是的。而你是——我的意思是1984年设计计算机芯片是什么样子的？是CAD吗？那是什么样子的——实际上物理上需要做什么？

turns.en: Yeah. Well, at the time I was the last generation of chip designers that did it by hand and the first generation of chip designers that use software to design computers, to design chips that ran in the computers that ran software. And so it was an incredible time. The perspective at the time—the chip I was working on had a few thousand transistors. And now we design chips that are 200 billion, a trillion transistors.
turns.zh: 是的。嗯，当时我是最后一代手工设计芯片的设计师，也是第一代使用软件设计计算机、设计芯片的设计师，这些芯片运行在运行软件的计算机中。所以那是一个不可思议的时代。当时的视角——我工作的芯片有几千个晶体管。而现在我们设计的芯片有2000亿、1万亿个晶体管。

turns.en: Insane.
turns.zh: 太疯狂了。

turns.en: Yeah. So the scale of the problems that we work on now compared to where we started is incredible. But anyhow, my office mate went to work for a startup company called LSI Logic. And that startup company—I didn't know anything about it. And she called me and said, hey, this is really quite a special company. You got to come take a look. And so I went to take a look at LSI Logic and it turned out this is an extraordinary company and completely revolutionary in what they were doing. Really in a lot of ways invented the modern way of designing chips. And so I got there, I joined them. I guess I was probably employee number 150 or 170 or something like that.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我们现在处理的问题规模与起步时相比是不可思议的。但不管怎样，我的办公室伙伴去了一家叫LSI Logic的初创公司工作。那家初创公司——我对此一无所知。她打电话给我说，嘿，这真的是一家非常特别的公司。你得来看看。所以我去看了LSI Logic，结果发现这是一家非凡的公司，他们所做的事情完全是革命性的。在很多方面真正发明了现代芯片设计方式。所以我去了那里，加入了他们。我猜我大概是第150或170号员工之类的。

turns.en: And you were like 22 probably at the time.
turns.zh: 你当时大概22岁吧。

turns.en: Yeah, I was just a kid. I was just a kid yeah. And I happened to join a revolutionary company at a perfect time and it really shaped how I think about technology.
turns.zh: 是的，我只是个孩子。我只是个孩子，是的。我碰巧在完美的时间加入了一家革命性的公司，这真的塑造了我对技术的思考方式。

turns.en: And from what I've read, I mean they
turns.zh: 从我读到的内容来看，我的意思是他们

turns.en: So far my life has been just one stroke of luck after another yeah.
turns.zh: 到目前为止，我的人生就是一连串的运气，是的。

turns.en: They gave you a lot of responsibility. I mean they—I mean you were eventually you would be in charge of tooling right? Like that was sort of
turns.zh: 他们给了你很多责任。我的意思是他们——我的意思是你最终会负责工具，对吧？就像那是某种

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: what you oversaw.
turns.zh: 你所监督的。

turns.en: The way LSI Logic's business worked is they had all the technology, the tools and they made the chips. But they would make it for somebody else who created computers. And so Sun Microsystems and Silicon Graphics and incredible companies at the time in Silicon Valley who were systems companies but they needed a chip company to help them build the chips. And so the CEO of LSI Logic and the executive that I worked for, Brian Halla, recognized my talents and put me in front of all these companies to help them translate their idea of what a computer is into a chip that we would build for them.
turns.zh: LSI Logic的商业模式是他们拥有所有技术、工具，他们制造芯片。但他们是为其他制造计算机的人制造。所以太阳微系统公司和硅谷图形公司以及当时硅谷那些不可思议的公司，它们是系统公司，但它们需要一家芯片公司来帮助它们制造芯片。所以LSI Logic的CEO和我为之工作的主管布莱恩·哈拉认可了我的才能，把我推到所有这些公司面前，帮助他们将他们对计算机的想法转化为我们将为他们制造的芯片。

turns.en: Mm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And so I spent a lot of time on campus at Sun Microsystems and Silicon Graphics and a whole bunch of other companies that were being started at the time. And I met some incredible people. They were history's brightest computer architects and I was just a kid. And I learned a ton from them and that again it was just an incredible stroke of luck that I had that perfect combination of knowledge and skills and put me in front of some really amazing people.
turns.zh: 所以我花了很多时间在太阳微系统公司和硅谷图形公司以及当时正在创办的一大批其他公司的园区里。我遇到了一些不可思议的人。他们是历史上最聪明的计算机架构师，而我只是个孩子。我从他们身上学到了很多，那又是一个不可思议的运气，我拥有知识和技能的完美结合，让我接触到了一些真正了不起的人。

turns.en: Two of those people that you met, um, Curtis Priem and Chris, were at Sun, and you had met them, I think, pretty early. And you were—I mean, this is sort of like the PC boom, the clone wars. I mean, there was a lot of demand for what LSI was producing, right? And it was an exciting time to be here, to be young, and to watch—you know, probably the next most exciting time would happen with the internet boom, right?
turns.zh: 你遇到的那些人中的两位，嗯，Curtis Priem 和 Chris，当时在 Sun，你遇到他们，我想，挺早的。而你当时——我是说，这有点像 PC 热潮、克隆战争。我是说，LSI 生产的东西需求很大，对吧？那是一个激动人心的时期，在这里，年轻，看着——你知道，下一个最激动人心的时期可能是互联网热潮，对吧？

turns.en: Well, LSI Logic was an extraordinary company because it happened at precisely the time—exactly as you're saying—that many, many computers, many supercomputers, all of those types of giant systems were being created by companies like Digital. And then the PC revolution started. And so we happened to be the company that helped everybody with their systems ideas, translate their system ideas into chips. And so I was really in the right place at the right time, and I saw new industries being created, worked with a whole bunch of amazing computer scientists. I saw a lot of great startups, and I was able to see firsthand companies being built and smart ideas, great technology, bad strategy, moderate technology, excellent strategy. I saw it all. I mean, it was quite an incredible thing. And then, of course, I met Chris and Curtis.
turns.zh: 嗯，LSI Logic 是一家非凡的公司，因为它恰好出现在——正如你所说——许多许多计算机、许多超级计算机，所有那些类型的巨型系统正由 Digital 等公司创造的时候。然后 PC 革命开始了。所以我们恰好是那家帮助所有人把系统想法转化为芯片的公司。所以我真的在正确的时间出现在了正确的地点，我看到了新产业被创造出来，与一大群了不起的计算机科学家共事。我看到了很多伟大的初创公司，我能够亲眼目睹公司如何建立，以及聪明的想法、伟大的技术、糟糕的战略，平庸的技术、卓越的战略。我全都看到了。我是说，那真是不可思议。然后，当然，我遇到了 Chris 和 Curtis。

turns.en: So going back to Chris and Curtis, the story is that these guys wanted to create at Sun Microsystems a chip specifically for games, for computer graphics, for games, and were rebuffed. And so, as often is the case, they decided to start their own company.
turns.zh: 那么回到 Chris 和 Curtis，故事是这样的：这些人想在 Sun Microsystems 创造一款专门用于游戏、用于计算机图形、用于游戏的芯片，但被拒绝了。所以，就像经常发生的那样，他们决定创办自己的公司。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And they approached you and they wanted you to work with them. And this is around 1992, '93. And from what I understand, I mean, you had a great job, you were well paid, you were well on the path to upper management. Like, this could have been a great stable career. You already had, I think, at least one kid at that time.
turns.zh: 他们找到了你，想让你和他们一起工作。这大约是 1992、93 年。据我所知，我是说，你有一份很棒的工作，薪水很高，你正处于通往高管的道路上。这本来可以是一个伟大而稳定的职业生涯。我记得你那时至少已经有一个孩子了。

turns.en: Yeah. Spencer Madison, yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。Spencer 和 Madison，是的。

turns.en: Um, and your wife was looking after the kids, so everyone depended on your salary. Um, and also you know—
turns.zh: 嗯，你的妻子在照顾孩子，所以每个人都依赖你的薪水。嗯，而且你知道——

turns.en: I think we had a whopping $30,000 in the bank, you know.
turns.zh: 我想我们银行里只有区区 3 万美元，你知道。

turns.en: And also your parents had immigrated to the United States. I imagine that they loved that you had this stable job, you had health insurance, and you had a retirement plan, and all these things. And maybe that was part of your psychology. Um, when they initially approached you, I mean, did you think that I'm not going to take that risk, I'm not going to leave this amazing job?
turns.zh: 而且你的父母移民到了美国。我想他们很喜欢你有一份稳定的工作，有医疗保险，有退休计划，所有这些。也许那是你心理的一部分。嗯，当他们最初找你时，我是说，你有没有想过我不会冒这个险，我不会离开这份了不起的工作？

turns.en: Yeah, I mean, they wanted to leave their jobs for the reasons you mentioned. I was happy with my job. And I—but they didn't give up asking me. And they were trying to figure out, so what should we do? You know.
turns.zh: 是的，我是说，他们想离开他们的工作，原因你提到了。我对我的工作很满意。而我——但他们没有放弃问我。他们试图弄清楚，那我们该做什么？你知道。

turns.en: Cuz they wanted you to run their—this business that they had an idea for.
turns.zh: 因为他们想让你经营他们——他们有一个想法的这个业务。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, there was an idea. I think that the basic idea was really computer graphics. In retrospect, the technology was clearly wrong. But nonetheless, Chris and Curtis are two of the brightest minds that I've ever met, brilliant engineers, incredible computer scientists. And so all the time that we spent trying to figure out—is there an opportunity here? Could we create a company?—the more we spoke about it, the more they asked me about it, the more I thought about it, the more excited I got about it myself. But I think ultimately, what did we really get excited about? In the end, what we got excited about was probably just the piece of revolution. We had that here's the first time a computer was going to be general purpose and you're going to use it for all kinds of different applications. And if it had computer graphics like what people were seeing with Jurassic Park and Silicon Graphics, and if we could figure out a way to make it affordable and architect something that would fit into a personal computer architecture, maybe there's a company here. I mean, in the end, that was probably just a simple big idea.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。是的，有一个想法。我认为基本的想法确实是计算机图形。 retrospect，技术显然是错误的。但尽管如此，Chris 和 Curtis 是我见过的最聪明的两个人，杰出的工程师，不可思议的计算机科学家。所以我们花的所有时间试图弄清楚——这里有机会吗？我们能创建一家公司吗？——我们谈论得越多，他们问我越多，我思考得越多，我自己就越兴奋。但我想最终，我们真正兴奋的是什么？最后，我们兴奋的可能只是那场革命。我们有了这个：这是第一次计算机将变得通用，你将把它用于各种不同的应用。如果它有像人们在《侏罗纪公园》和 Silicon Graphics 中看到的计算机图形，如果我们能想办法让它变得可负担，并设计出适合个人计算机架构的东西，也许这里有一家公司。我是说，最后，那可能只是一个简单的大想法。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Almost—that was the initial seed of what we were excited about. Everything about the company that manifested from that point is really where the great strategies came from. I would say, almost like everything else in life, you start down a journey and you find new paths from it. But that initial step on the trail, whatever the inspiration was that took us there—it was a good idea. It was a good idea. We expanded it. It was good that we expanded the idea.
turns.zh: 几乎——那就是我们兴奋的最初种子。从那时起公司所展现的一切，真正是伟大战略的来源。我想说，几乎像生活中的其他一切一样，你开始一段旅程，然后从中找到新的路径。但旅程上的第一步，无论是什么灵感带我们到那里——那是一个好主意。那是一个好主意。我们扩展了它。我们扩展了这个想法，这很好。

turns.en: But I mean at the time there were like 60 companies trying to do this, right? And so clearly you had confidence in these guys and you knew they were smart. But you know, you're 29, 30 and you got this great job and a couple of kids. And so you took the leap, obviously, to start this company with them. But what do you remember—I mean, imagine your wife was supportive. She said go for it.
turns.zh: 但我是说，当时大约有 60 家公司在尝试做这个，对吧？所以显然你对这些人有信心，你知道他们很聪明。但你知道，你 29、30 岁，有一份很棒的工作和几个孩子。所以你显然迈出了这一步，和他们一起创办了这家公司。但你记得什么——我是说，想象你的妻子是支持的。她说去吧。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: So was there any part of you—do you remember any part of you thinking, God, what if this doesn't work out?
turns.zh: 所以你是否有任何一部分——你记得有任何一部分在想，天啊，如果这不行怎么办？

turns.en: No. Yeah, I should have. It didn't really. No. I guess you were prepared for whatever happened would happen.
turns.zh: 没有。是的，我应该（担心）。但并没有。没有。我想你准备好了无论发生什么都会发生。

turns.en: Yeah. And whatever the consequence is, the consequences.
turns.zh: 是的。无论后果是什么，就是后果。

turns.en: Yeah, you get another job. I mean, what's the worst case that you get another job? I think—no, it never once crossed my mind that it wouldn't work out. You know, once—it's kind of a weird thing. Once an idea manifests and you think about it and you imagine it and you obsess about it, before you know it, it becomes a reality that is as real as anything else.
turns.zh: 是的，你再找一份工作。我是说，最坏的情况不就是你再找一份工作吗？我想——不，我从未想过它不会成功。你知道，一旦——这有点奇怪。一旦一个想法显现，你思考它，想象它，痴迷于它，不知不觉中，它变成了一个和其他任何现实一样真实的现实。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And maybe that's what's called vision. Maybe that's where determination comes from. But NVIDIA manifested in my mind, and an industry manifested in my mind, that was so crystal clear. I never once did it cross my mind it wouldn't work out. And of course, you know, didn't work out but—
turns.zh: 也许那就是所谓的愿景。也许决心就来自那里。但 NVIDIA 在我脑海中显现，一个产业在我脑海中显现，如此清晰。我从未想过它不会成功。当然，你知道，并没有成功，但——

turns.en: Well, didn't right. So NVIDIA is the company which I guess comes from the Latin word envy, NVIDIA. And you guys start working on the first product, which is going to be a revolutionary graphics processing chip that is going to make—
turns.zh: 嗯，没有成功，对。所以 NVIDIA 是这家公司，我猜来自拉丁词 envy，NVIDIA。你们开始研发第一款产品，那将是一款革命性的图形处理芯片，它将使——

turns.en: We were the first 3D graphics company in the world that started with the idea that we bring 3D graphics to consumers.
turns.zh: 我们是世界上第一家以将 3D 图形带给消费者为理念而起步的 3D 图形公司。

turns.en: So that bought and so 1993 it's founded and you start to work on this product
turns.zh: 所以那笔交易，然后 1993 年公司成立，你们开始研发这款产品

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: and you guys raise a little bit of money
turns.zh: 你们筹了一点钱

turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 没有。

turns.en: to do it. And this is going to be a game changer, right? I mean this is going to be like the coolest thing
turns.zh: 来做这件事。这会改变游戏规则，对吧？我是说这会是最酷的东西

turns.en: Yeah, we thought so. Yeah, we thought so. The technology we created allowed us to generate images but using a lot less electronics, a lot fewer chips and a lot more affordable than these giant supercomputers that Silicon Graphics was making at the time. You know, at the time the computer that generated images for Jurassic Park would cost, you know, a million dollars at the time and we needed to get something to fit into about 300 bucks and so that leap, that transformation and yet generate beautiful images that gap was so large that we had to reinvent the algorithms all together. And it turned out the algorithms that we invented, you know, were just flawed.
turns.zh: 是的，我们当时是这么想的。是的，我们当时是这么想的。我们创造的技术让我们能够生成图像，但使用的电子元件少得多，芯片少得多，而且比当时 Silicon Graphics 制造的巨型超级计算机便宜得多。你知道，当时为《侏罗纪公园》生成图像的计算机要花费一百万美元，而我们需要做出一个大约 300 美元的东西。所以那个飞跃、那个转变，同时还要生成精美的图像，那个差距太大了，我们不得不彻底重新发明算法。结果我们发现，我们发明的算法就是有缺陷的。

turns.en: I mean it sold well initially. I think there's a lot of excitement about it.

turns.en: And so in fact, the NVIDIA journey every single step of the way, we were always the disruptor. So I think the large lesson of Clay Christensen is really about disruption and how technology emerges out of thin air that apparently looks like toys but went off to disrupt large markets. For us to scare them into not even wanting to go to college, okay, not even wanting to be a computer scientist is a disservice to society. You're not saving anybody. You're not warning anybody. You're talking a whole bunch of people into out of professions that we need in the future.
turns.zh: 部分是的。我认为部分是的。我相信，今天计算机科学、计算机工程、软件工程或芯片设计专业的新毕业生所拥有的机会和潜力，远比我毕业时要大得多。他们可用的工具能力要强十亿倍。如今使用 EDA 已经高度自动化。然而他们比以往更忙。他们比以往更抢手。原因在于，我们有了想要构建的东西的想法，而这些想法在没有我们现有工具的时代是无法想象的。AI 将帮助下一代新毕业生取得伟大成就，构建更伟大的东西，而不是夺走他们的工作。我们吓唬他们，让他们甚至不想上大学，好吧，甚至不想成为计算机科学家，这是对社会的伤害。你救不了任何人。你警告不了任何人。你是在把一大堆人劝退，让他们离开我们未来需要的职业。

turns.en: Hm. And that conversation is not happening in China?
turns.zh: 嗯。那种对话在中国没有发生吗？

turns.en: They're not buying it. They're just not buying it.
turns.zh: 他们不买账。他们就是不买账。

turns.en: Hm. Do you think that there is a possibility that in 10 years from now NVIDIA will have an order of magnitude more employees?
turns.zh: 嗯。你认为有没有可能，10 年后 NVIDIA 的员工数量会多一个数量级？

turns.en: Before AI or after AI, I don't think it would make any difference. The difference is that with AI along with my employees, we're going to have hundreds, thousands of AI assistants helping them do amazing things. And so our expectations of our company will be different. How long it takes me to do something, how incredible it takes to do something, my expectation has already changed.
turns.zh: 在 AI 之前还是之后，我认为不会有任何区别。区别在于，有了 AI，和我的员工一起，我们将有数百、数千个 AI 助手帮助他们做了不起的事情。因此，我们对公司的期望会不同。我做一件事需要多长时间，做一件事能有多不可思议，我的期望已经改变了。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Things that take 10 years, I think will take 1 year.
turns.zh: 过去需要 10 年的事情，我认为将只需要 1 年。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And so is that good or bad? It's just thrilling. It's exhilarating, I think.
turns.zh: 那么这是好是坏？这很激动人心。我认为这令人兴奋。

turns.en: I know that you don't like to talk about speculation, and that makes a lot of sense. But I read an excerpt from a new book that's coming out. It's called Defending Taiwan by a writer named Ike Freeman. And he paints a scenario of a possible conflict, hot conflict where all of a sudden Taiwan is somehow invaded or occupied, whatever you want to call it, right? And we've seen what, you know, we've got some challenges geopolitically, right? What I mean, what part of that, let's just say that scenario is not realistic, right? That it would be destructive for China as well because their economy really depends on the US market. Does any part of the fact that such a high percentage of advanced chips, not just NVIDIA, but advanced chips are produced in Taiwan? Is any part of that? Should people be concerned about that at all?
turns.zh: 我知道你不喜欢谈论猜测，这很有道理。但我读了一本即将出版的新书的摘录。书名叫《保卫台湾》，作者是艾克·弗里曼。他描绘了一个可能冲突的场景，热冲突，突然间台湾以某种方式被入侵或占领，随便你怎么称呼，对吧？我们已经看到，你知道，我们在地缘政治上面临一些挑战，对吧？我的意思是，那个场景的哪一部分，我们就说那个场景不现实，对吧？那对中国也具有破坏性，因为他们的经济确实依赖美国市场。那么，如此高比例的先进芯片，不仅仅是 NVIDIA 的，而是先进芯片在台湾生产，这个事实的哪一部分？人们应该对此感到担忧吗？

turns.en: I wish we always have a resilient supply chain. That's part of building a strong company. You should have resilient supply chains. And a resilient supply chain has diversity and redundancy. And so to the best of your ability, you build a company that has diversity and redundancy. There are many companies that are built only on Windows. It runs completely on Windows. There are companies that are completely run on iPhones. There are companies that are built that completely run on AWS. It is better to have diversity and redundancy. But you also know that sometimes you don't have the benefit of diversity and redundancy. So you make the best you can. I think there are a lot of conflated questions that are put into that concern.
turns.zh: 我希望我们始终拥有一个有韧性的供应链。这是建立强大公司的一部分。你应该有有韧性的供应链。而有韧性的供应链具有多样性和冗余性。因此，尽你所能，建立一家具有多样性和冗余性的公司。有许多公司只建立在 Windows 上。它完全在 Windows 上运行。有些公司完全在 iPhone 上运行。有些公司完全在 AWS 上运行。拥有多样性和冗余性更好。但你也知道，有时你无法享受多样性和冗余性的好处。所以你尽力而为。我认为那个担忧中混杂了许多被混为一谈的问题。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And if you ask me, am I concerned about a hot conflict? I'm less concerned than most. And depending on the actions of the leaders, we may cause the hot conflict. And so I am of the opinion that we all must be more long-term minded if we can. We ought to have a more balanced and nuanced set of policies. Not all or nothing. Don't push your adversaries, don't push your competitors to the wall where they have no choice or where there's no cost to a strategic alternative. And so I think that in your question, do I believe it? The answer is I don't. I don't believe it because I believe can it happen? Of course it can happen everywhere obviously. However, I believe in the wisdom of the people involved.
turns.zh: 如果你问我，我是否担心热冲突？我比大多数人更不担心。而且取决于领导人的行动，我们可能引发热冲突。所以我的观点是，如果可以，我们所有人都必须更有长远眼光。我们应该有一套更平衡、更微妙的政策。不是全有或全无。不要把你的对手、不要把你的竞争者逼到墙角，让他们别无选择，或者让战略替代方案没有成本。所以我认为，在你的问题中，我相信它会发生吗？答案是不。我不相信，因为我相信——它可能发生吗？当然，显然在任何地方都可能发生。然而，我相信相关人士的智慧。

turns.en: What have you had to unlearn as a leader? The bigger this company has gotten and the more experienced you've gotten. I mean you are known for being hard demanding, hard charging. You demand the best out of people. You have yelled at people, all those things. Would you say those things are still how you manage or have you unlearned some of those things or have you changed some of those things in your style?
turns.zh: 作为领导者，你不得不摒弃了什么？随着公司越来越大，你越来越有经验。我的意思是，你以严厉、要求高、拼命著称。你要求人们做到最好。你曾对人大吼，所有那些事情。你会说那些仍然是你管理的方式，还是你已经摒弃了其中一些，或者在你的风格中改变了其中一些？

turns.en: I think the company doesn't—I don't think people care about style. I think people care about your values and what you care about. So long as you're tough on the same things every time it comes up.
turns.zh: 我认为公司并不——我认为人们不在乎风格。我认为人们在乎你的价值观和你在乎什么。只要每次出现同样的事情时你都坚持原则。

turns.en: So long as the moment that it's over, it's over and they know that they're safe, you love them, you want them to succeed. This is their life's work and you want it to be as good as it can be. Everybody knows that I have enough of everything. Whatever it is that anybody thinks they need more of, I've got plenty of it.
turns.zh: 只要那一刻结束了，就结束了，他们知道自己是安全的，你爱他们，你希望他们成功。这是他们毕生的事业，你希望它尽可能好。大家都知道我什么都有够。无论任何人认为他们需要更多什么，我都有很多。

turns.en: Hm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And yet I work harder than ever. And the reason for that is because I want everything that I have, they have. I want them to see to realize their dreams. And I feel that about our company. I feel that about my partners. I feel that about the companies that we work with that helped me get here. And so long as you're pure and high integrity and completely for them, you could be challenging to people and they know that you're on their side.
turns.zh: 然而我比以往任何时候都更努力。原因是我希望我所拥有的一切，他们也能拥有。我希望他们看到并实现自己的梦想。我对我们公司有这种感觉。我对我的合作伙伴有这种感觉。我对那些帮助我们走到今天的合作公司有这种感觉。只要你纯粹、正直，完全为他们着想，你可能会对人要求严格，但他们知道你是站在他们这边的。

turns.en: Now would you say that all of those things you mentioned, people you met and the decisions that were made, the good decisions and the bad ones and the grind and the result now, the most— I mean you hear it a million times and it's probably still crazy to hear— at the most valuable company in the world, right? I mean the value of this company is bigger than most countries by far. Do you think that that happened because of all of those elements, all the people, the hard work, the grind or do you think that luck played a bigger role?
turns.zh: 现在，你会说所有你提到的那些事情，你遇到的人，做出的决定，好的决定和坏的决定，以及辛勤工作和现在的结果，最——我的意思是，你听过无数次，但听到可能仍然觉得疯狂——在世界上最有价值的公司，对吧？我的意思是，这家公司的价值远远超过大多数国家。你认为这一切的发生是因为所有这些因素，所有的人，努力工作，辛勤付出，还是你认为运气起了更大的作用？

turns.en: Several hundred forks in the road in a lifetime. I've largely taken the right one. Combination of good judgment, good values, good friends, informed decisions, critical thinking and some dose of luck led me to choosing the best of several options. And when the company didn't choose the best options, we created a system that allowed it to self-reflect, to not take ourselves too seriously, to not be so hard on ourselves for making a bad decision that we can quickly adjust. And not let the bad decision be fatal. I've read a lot of business books, I've read a lot of strategy books. I'm informed by a lot of them. But I think that in the end, I think the secret to it all, you know, the only thing I've really learned about it all is that the next fork in the road is about to come. And the people that are going to help me make the best decisions likely will be different than the ones that helped me make the last decisions. You got to figure out who they are. And I've always felt safe making strategic decisions. I've always felt safe taking risks.
turns.zh: 一生中有几百个岔路口。我基本上都选对了。良好的判断力、良好的价值观、好朋友、明智的决策、批判性思维以及一些运气，这些结合起来让我在几个选项中选择了最好的。当公司没有选择最佳选项时，我们建立了一个系统，允许自我反思，不把自己太当回事，不因为做出错误决定而对自己太苛刻，以便快速调整。并且不让错误决定成为致命伤。我读过很多商业书籍，读过很多战略书籍。我从中学到很多。但我认为最终，这一切的秘诀，你知道，我真正学到的唯一一点是，下一个岔路口即将到来。而帮助我做出最佳决策的人很可能与帮助我做出上一次决策的人不同。你得弄清楚他们是谁。而且我一直觉得做出战略决策是安全的。我一直觉得冒险是安全的。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Maybe it's because I know that when I get home, Lori's still there. You know? Maybe it's because when I get home, I know the kids are there. Maybe I know that all of our employees are going to be here because they want me to succeed. Maybe that is as complicated as it is. I wish I could be more technical in explaining how companies are built and run. But I built this one from the first day and it's much more personal, I frankly believe. You know, because people say and it's not business, it's personal. It's always personal.
turns.zh: 也许是因为我知道当我回家时，洛丽还在那里。你知道吗？也许是因为当我回家时，我知道孩子们在那里。也许我知道我们所有的员工都会在这里，因为他们希望我成功。也许就是这么复杂。我希望我能更技术性地解释公司是如何建立和运营的。但我从第一天就建立了这个公司，坦率地说，它更加个人化。你知道，因为人们说这不是业务，这是个人的。它总是个人的。

turns.en: James, thank you.
turns.zh: 詹姆斯，谢谢你。

turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

consensus.en: Greatness requires enduring pain and suffering; you must forget yesterday to keep moving forward.
consensus.zh: 伟大需要忍受痛苦与磨难；必须忘记昨天才能继续前行。

consensus.en: NVIDIA's success came from first-principles thinking and building a resilient, diverse supply chain.
consensus.zh: NVIDIA 的成功源于第一性原理思考和构建有韧性、多元化的供应链。

consensus.en: CUDA's strategy was to carry it on GeForce to every computer, sacrificing margins for decades.
consensus.zh: CUDA 的策略是借助 GeForce 将其带到每台电脑，牺牲利润数十年。

consensus.en: AI will create more opportunities, not destroy jobs; radiologists demand increased after AI.
consensus.zh: AI 将创造更多机会而非摧毁工作；AI 之后放射科医生需求反而增加。

consensus.en: Leaders should be tough on values, not style; people care about your integrity and care.
consensus.zh: 领导者应在价值观上严格而非风格；人们在乎你的正直与关怀。

consensus.en: The secret to success is recognizing the next fork in the road and choosing the right people.
consensus.zh: 成功的秘诀是识别下一个岔路口并选择正确的人。

contrarian.en: I would not start NVIDIA again knowing the pain; most people answering yes are dishonest.
contrarian.zh: 知道痛苦后我不会再创办 NVIDIA；大多数回答“会”的人不诚实。

contrarian.en: AI alarmism is harmful; we should speed up innovation, not slow it down.
contrarian.zh: AI 恐慌论有害；我们应加速创新而非放缓。

contrarian.en: The greatest AI risk is the US scaring people into not using it, not existential threat.
contrarian.zh: AI 最大风险是美国吓唬人们不使用它，而非生存威胁。

contrarian.en: Job has purpose and task; AI automates tasks but purpose remains, expanding demand.
contrarian.zh: 工作有目的和任务；AI 自动化任务但目的仍在，需求扩大。

contrarian.en: I'm less concerned about a hot conflict over Taiwan than most; leaders' actions matter.
contrarian.zh: 我比大多数人更不担心台湾热战；领导人的行动很重要。

contrarian.en: Staying the course was not hard; giving up would have been harder.
contrarian.zh: 坚持到底并不难；放弃反而更难。
